pool.label: C1
pool.builds_on: The paper’s demonstration of a temperature-dependent clustering driven by Al–Ni interactions and the identification of a spinodal temperature (~840 K) (PMC4976365::web::007).
pool.what_is_new: This hypothesis explicitly links thermal treatment (holding below versus above a key temperature) to phase stability via modulation of atomic clustering, and it connects those microstructural differences to tangible high-temperature and environmental performance metrics.

fields.hypothesis: Phase stability is governed by a temperature‐dependent competition between short-range ordering driven by dominant pair interactions (e.g., Al–Ni clustering) and the mixing entropy that stabilizes a random solid solution. In practice, holding the alloy isothermally at temperatures below the spinodal temperature (~840 K) promotes clustering, whereas maintaining high processing temperatures or rapid quenching preserves disorder. This balance ultimately affects high-temperature strength and oxidation (environmental) resistance.
fields.material_initial_state: A melt‐quenched Al–Co–Cr–Fe–Ni HEA (e.g., with Al mole fraction x = 0.1) in its metastable single‐phase FCC (A1) state that exhibits evidence of Al–Ni driven clustering as indicated by SRO parameters.
fields.intervention: Prepare two sets of identical HEA samples. For one group, apply an isothermal hold (annealing) at a temperature below ~840 K (e.g., 750 K) for a controlled duration to promote atomic clustering. For the other group, either rapidly quench from the melt or anneal at a temperature moderately above 840 K to maintain a more random disordered state.
fields.conditions: Identical composition (Al0.1CrCoFeNi) and processing history except for the controlled thermal treatment; testing to be performed at room and elevated temperatures (e.g., 300–700 K) for mechanical (flow stress) and oxidation resistance assessments.
fields.structural_mediator: The degree of short-range order (SRO) as quantified by pair correlation functions (e.g., intensity of Al–Ni and Al–Al peaks) measured via diffraction or atom probe techniques.
fields.mechanism: At temperatures below the spinodal threshold, the favorable chemical interchange energies (as evidenced in the KKR-CPA analysis, PMC4976365::web::007) overcome the mixing entropy, driving clustering of like pairs. In contrast, rapid quenching or annealing above this threshold preserves a more homogeneous atomic distribution. The local atomic arrangement influences free volume distribution and potential nucleation sites for oxidation, thereby impacting high-temperature mechanical strength and environmental resistance.
fields.predicted_outcome: Samples annealed below 840 K will show enhanced clustering (stronger Al–Ni and Al–Al pair peaks) and may exhibit slightly reduced high-temperature flow stress and lower oxidation resistance compared to the rapidly quenched or high-temperature held samples. The baseline (rapidly quenched) samples are predicted to have a more uniform disordered structure with improved performance in high-temperature environments.
fields.baseline: Al0.1CrCoFeNi HEA processed by rapid quenching, retaining the high-temperature disordered (entropy-stabilized) state.
fields.boundary: This temperature-dependent mechanism applies to the single-phase FCC (A1) regime with low Al content (x = 0.1) and assumes that thermal treatments do not trigger full phase separation or induce unwanted secondary phases beyond a limited clustering regime.
fields.uncertainty: The quantitative differences in mechanical or oxidation properties between the two states may be modest, and the precise temperature window over which the crossover occurs requires refinement; current support is robust for clustering trends but less so for direct property correlations.

falsification_experiment.design: Prepare two groups of Al0.1CrCoFeNi samples: one subjected to an isothermal hold at 750 K for a fixed time and one rapidly quenched. Characterize the short-range order using high-resolution diffraction or atom probe tomography. Then, measure high-temperature flow stress and oxidation resistance under identical test conditions.
measurements: SRO parameters from pair correlation data (e.g., Al–Ni, Al–Al peaks)
High-temperature mechanical properties (flow stress, yield strength)
Oxidation rate or passivation behavior tests
falsification_experiment.falsification_rule: If no significant difference in SRO and corresponding high-temperature mechanical and oxidation properties is observed between the annealed and rapidly quenched samples, then the temperature-dependent control of phase stability is falsified.

pool.label: C2
pool.builds_on: The paper shows that oxidation behavior in AlCoCrFeNi HEA is sensitive to element distributions and microstructural features (PMC9498035::web::009 and PMC9498035::web::021).
pool.what_is_new: This hypothesis specifically targets controlled grain-boundary segregation via tailored heat treatment as a means to enhance the continuity of protective oxide scales, addressing high-temperature phase stability directly—without invoking additional effects beyond those observed in the paper.

fields.hypothesis: Tailoring heat-treatment conditions to promote grain-boundary enrichment of Al and Cr in polycrystalline Al–Co–Cr–Fe–Ni HEA will result in a more continuous and coherent protective oxide scale (mainly α-Al2O3 and Cr2O3) during high-temperature exposure, thereby stabilizing the phase by retarding internal oxidation and associated degradation.
fields.material_initial_state: Polycrystalline Al–Co–Cr–Fe–Ni HEA produced by conventional casting and homogenization, exhibiting random distribution of elements with natural grain boundaries.
fields.intervention: Apply a sub-transus anneal with a prolonged hold at an intermediate temperature designed to drive modest segregation of Al and Cr to grain boundaries without inducing deleterious secondary phase formation.
fields.conditions: Compare samples receiving the segregation-enhancing heat treatment to baseline samples subjected to standard homogenization. Expose both sets to high-temperature oxidation (e.g., 1000 K) for a controlled duration.
fields.structural_mediator: Grain boundaries enriched in passivating elements (Al and Cr) that serve as nucleation sites for a contiguous oxide scale.
fields.mechanism: Enrichment of Al and Cr at grain boundaries lowers the local oxidation potential and accelerates the formation of continuous α-Al2O3 and Cr2O3 layers. These coherent oxide films act as slow-diffusion barriers, reducing further oxygen ingress and internal oxidation—a key factor in maintaining phase stability at high temperatures.
fields.predicted_outcome: The treated alloy is expected to display a thinner and more continuous oxide scale with reduced internal oxidation and improved phase stability under high-temperature exposure compared to the baseline. Improvements are expected in oxidation kinetics and microstructural integrity (though the precise magnitude must be determined experimentally).
fields.baseline: Alloy processed by standard homogenization, with no specific enhancement of grain-boundary segregation.
fields.boundary: This hypothesis is applicable to polycrystalline HEAs where grain-boundary chemistry can be modified; it does not extend to single-crystal or ultra-fine-grained materials where segregation effects are minimal.
fields.uncertainty: The optimum heat-treatment parameters to achieve effective segregation without causing unwanted phase coarsening remain to be determined.

falsification_experiment.design: Prepare two sets of polycrystalline Al–Co–Cr–Fe–Ni HEA: one with the tailored segregation-enhancing heat treatment and one with conventional homogenization. Use high-resolution SEM/EDS or atom probe tomography to assess grain-boundary compositions. Subject both sets to 1000 K oxidation for a fixed time, then use TEM and XPS to evaluate oxide scale continuity, thickness, and composition.
measurements: Grain-boundary composition (Al and Cr levels)
Oxide scale morphology and continuity (TEM, SEM)
Oxide thickness and kinetics (thermogravimetric analysis)
falsification_experiment.falsification_rule: If the treated samples do not exhibit significantly higher grain-boundary Al/Cr enrichment, nor a more continuous/coherent protective oxide scale, or if the oxidation kinetics and phase stability are not improved relative to the baseline, the hypothesis is falsified.

pool.label: C3
pool.builds_on: The paper and background literature indicate that grain boundaries play a key role in diffusion-controlled oxidation processes (PMC9498035::web::011; TXT::wikipedia::Superalloy::002).
pool.what_is_new: This hypothesis shifts the focus from chemical segregation to grain size engineering as a controlling factor for oxidation behavior and phase stability, extending the paper’s microstructural insights into a processing-driven intervention.

fields.hypothesis: Reducing the average grain size in Al–Co–Cr–Fe–Ni HEA via controlled thermomechanical processing will enhance high-temperature phase stability by accelerating the formation of protective oxides through increased grain-boundary diffusion of Al and Cr, thereby limiting internal oxidation and detrimental phase changes.
fields.material_initial_state: Al–Co–Cr–Fe–Ni HEA produced by conventional casting that typically contains a coarse-grained microstructure with standard diffusion pathways.
fields.intervention: Apply a thermomechanical processing route (e.g., warm working followed by appropriate recrystallization annealing) aimed at reducing the grain size while maintaining a single-phase microstructure.
fields.conditions: Prepare a comparative study between a fine-grained processed HEA and an annealed, coarse-grained counterpart. Subject both sets to identical high-temperature oxidation tests (e.g., at 1000 K for 25 h).
fields.structural_mediator: Increased density of grain boundaries which serve as rapid diffusion paths for Al and Cr, enabling prompt formation of protective oxidic layers.
fields.mechanism: With a smaller grain size, the higher grain-boundary area facilitates faster transport of Al and Cr to the surface during oxidation. This enhanced diffusion promotes the early and uniform formation of α-Al2O3 and Cr2O3, creating an effective barrier against further oxidation and internal oxygen ingress. In turn, the reduced oxidation-induced degradation helps maintain the phase integrity required for high-temperature strength and environmental resistance.
fields.predicted_outcome: The fine-grained HEA is expected to exhibit a more uniform and continuous protective oxide scale, reduced oxide-scale thickness progression, and consequently better phase stability compared to the coarse-grained material. Quantitative improvements in oxidation resistance and microstructural preservation are anticipated.
fields.baseline: Coarse-grained HEA produced via standard cast-and-anneal processes.
fields.boundary: This hypothesis applies to processing routes that can reliably produce uniform fine grains without generating unwanted stress or texture that might independently affect oxidation processes.
fields.uncertainty: The optimum grain size that maximizes the beneficial effect on oxidation while avoiding adverse mechanical property changes requires further experimental optimization.

falsification_experiment.design: Process two sets of HEA samples: one using a thermomechanical route to achieve a fine-grained microstructure, and one conventional coarse-grained sample. Characterize grain size distributions with EBSD. Expose both samples to high-temperature oxidation at 1000 K for 25 h, and analyze the oxide scales using SEM/TEM and XRD. Compare oxidation kinetics and microstructural changes.
measurements: Grain size distribution (EBSD)
Oxide scale continuity and thickness (SEM, TEM)
Phase composition before and after oxidation (XRD)
falsification_experiment.falsification_rule: If the fine-grained samples do not show a significantly enhanced formation of continuous α-Al2O3/Cr2O3 layers and exhibit oxidation kinetics or phase degradation comparable to or worse than the coarse-grained samples, the hypothesis is falsified.

pool.label: C4
pool.builds_on: The paper’s finding that high configurational entropy in single-phase Al0.1CoCrFeNi suppresses precipitation by reducing diffusion and thermodynamic driving force.
pool.what_is_new: This hypothesis tests whether processing routes that further maximize configurational entropy—beyond just alloy composition control—can enhance phase stability, coupling processing-induced disorder with irradiation performance in application-relevant conditions.

fields.hypothesis: Enhancing phase stability by maximizing configurational entropy to kinetically suppress atomic diffusion and irradiation‐induced precipitation.
fields.material_initial_state: Al–Co–Cr–Fe–Ni high-entropy alloy initially processed to form a single-phase disordered fcc solid solution (e.g., with low Al content analogous to Al0.1CoCrFeNi).
fields.intervention: Process the alloy under rapid solidification conditions (e.g. splat quenching or high cooling rate casting) to further minimize any incipient elemental partitioning and promote a maximized configurational entropy state.
fields.conditions: Test under room temperature and moderate high-temperature (e.g., 300–400 °C) irradiation conditions using ion irradiation, with otherwise identical compositions; compare to conventionally solidified samples that may have initial short-range ordering.
fields.structural_mediator: Single-phase fcc matrix with low diffusion rates; absence of ordered intermetallic or phase separated regions.
fields.mechanism: High configurational entropy effectively lowers the thermodynamic driving force for the precipitation of secondary phases and, coupled with sluggish diffusion kinetics in the disordered matrix, retards the growth of defects or precipitates under irradiation. This stabilization mechanism should help retain high-temperature strength, radiation tolerance, and cryogenic toughness.
fields.predicted_outcome: The rapidly solidified alloy will display reduced or no detectable irradiation-induced precipitates compared to the conventionally processed baseline, with retention of high-temperature strength and toughness. The effect is predicted to be moderate-to-large, as even small differences in initial ordering can dramatically influence defect diffusion.
fields.baseline: Conventional cast or slowly cooled Al–Co–Cr–Fe–Ni alloy with similar composition but with a possible tendency toward short-range order or incipient phase separation.
fields.boundary: Valid for alloys with compositions close to the equiatomic regime and for irradiation conditions up to ~50 dpa and temperatures up to about 400 °C; the hypothesis may not hold if thermal treatments induce ordering prior to irradiation.
fields.uncertainty: Exact quantitative thresholds of configurational entropy and cooling rate required remain to be optimized.

falsification_experiment.design: Prepare two sets of Al–Co–Cr–Fe–Ni alloys: one rapidly solidified to enhance disorder and a conventionally cast variant. Subject both to identical ion irradiation up to 50 dpa at room temperature and an elevated temperature (e.g., 350 °C). Use TEM and diffraction techniques to quantify precipitate formation and measure mechanical properties (yield strength, toughness) before and after irradiation.
measurements: TEM imaging and SAED for phase identification
Nano-EDX/EELS for compositional homogeneity
Mechanical testing for high-temperature strength and cryogenic toughness
falsification_experiment.falsification_rule: If the rapidly solidified sample exhibits similar or enhanced precipitation (or degradation in mechanical properties) compared to the conventionally cast sample under identical conditions, then the hypothesis is falsified.

pool.label: C5
pool.builds_on: The paper’s demonstration of cellular and homogeneous precipitation of L12 particles in an Al-containing HEA and the known role of Al in promoting Ni3Al (γ') formation in superalloys.
pool.what_is_new: It proposes to tune phase stability and property combinations by adjusting composition to favor a homogeneous fine L12 dispersion rather than undesirable cellular precipitation, explicitly linking microstructural control to enhanced radiation tolerance and cryogenic toughness.

fields.hypothesis: A slight increase in Al content will enhance the chemical partitioning between the FCC matrix and the L12 precipitates, increasing the coherent L12 volume fraction and thus stabilizing the high‐temperature phase while simultaneously providing more effective defect sinks under irradiation.
fields.material_initial_state: An Al–Co–Cr–Fe–Ni high-entropy alloy with approximately equal atomic percentages that forms a single FCC phase after quenching, similar to the base Ni36Co18Cr20Fe19Al7 composition.
fields.intervention: Increase the Al content by about 2–3 at.% (within the HEA compositional limits) during alloy synthesis.
fields.conditions: Prepare two sets of alloys (baseline and Al-enhanced) using identical melting, homogenization, hot forging, cold rolling, and quenching procedures; then subject both sets to identical annealing treatments (e.g., isothermal holding at 873 K).
fields.structural_mediator: The formation of a higher volume fraction of fine, coherent L12 precipitates with a cuboidal or spherical morphology in the FCC matrix.
fields.mechanism: An increased Al content promotes the precipitation of Ni3(Al)-type (L12) particles by shifting the partitioning equilibrium. The fine coherent L12 particles act as obstacles to dislocation motion, which improves high-temperature strength, and also serve as sinks for irradiation-induced defects while maintaining a ductile FCC matrix that helps cryogenic toughness. However, the Al enrichment must be kept moderate to avoid promoting deleterious grain-boundary lamellar cellular precipitation that can compromise toughness.
fields.predicted_outcome: Compared to the baseline alloy, the Al-enhanced alloy will show a higher fraction of finely dispersed L12 precipitates, improved high-temperature strength (and creep resistance), enhanced radiation tolerance, and maintained or improved cryogenic toughness. The effect is expected to be on the order of a moderate (uncertain quantitative magnitude) shift in the precipitation volume fraction and mechanical property improvements.
fields.baseline: The original HEA formulation, where cellular precipitation produces both fine coherent L12 particles in the matrix and lamellar grain-boundary precipitates.
fields.boundary: Works when the Al increase remains within the solubility limits of the FCC phase to avoid unwanted formation of coarse brittle phases or excessive cellular precipitation at grain boundaries. May not hold if Al content is too high.
fields.uncertainty: Exact volume fraction changes and the quantitative improvement in in-service conditions remain to be determined experimentally.

falsification_experiment.design: Fabricate two sets of alloys—one with the baseline Al content and one with an increased Al content by 2–3 at.%. After identical heat treatments, map the precipitate distribution using TEM and perform high-temperature mechanical, irradiation, and low-temperature (cryogenic) toughness tests.
measurements: Volume fraction and size distribution of L12 precipitates (by TEM/EDS)
High-temperature yield strength/creep tests
Irradiation-induced defect density (via TEM) or related mechanical property degradation
Cryogenic toughness (impact or bend tests)
falsification_experiment.falsification_rule: If the Al-enhanced alloy does not exhibit a statistically significant increase in fine L12 precipitate fraction and corresponding enhancements in high-temperature strength, radiation tolerance, and cryogenic toughness compared to the baseline, the hypothesis is falsified.

pool.label: C6
pool.builds_on: The paper’s observation of both homogeneous and cellular precipitation in the HEA and the background understanding that heat treatment parameters critically affect precipitation mechanisms.
pool.what_is_new: It proposes a specific heat treatment modification to decouple the beneficial fine-particle precipitation from the deleterious cellular (grain-boundary) precipitation, with direct implications for balancing high-temperature and cryogenic performance.

fields.hypothesis: Tailoring the annealing heat treatment to favor homogeneous nucleation of fine L12 precipitates over grain-boundary cellular precipitation will stabilize the FCC matrix and yield a microstructure that balances high-temperature strength with improved cryogenic toughness and environmental resistance.
fields.material_initial_state: An Al–Co–Cr–Fe–Ni HEA that is initially single-phase FCC after rapid quenching, similar to the state reported in the referenced paper.
fields.intervention: Modify the annealing schedule by reducing the isothermal holding temperature (e.g., from 873 K to a lower temperature such as 773 K) or reducing holding time to suppress the kinetics of grain-boundary migration and cellular precipitation, thereby promoting homogeneous fine L12 precipitation.
fields.conditions: Prepare parallel samples from the same alloy batch; subject one set to the baseline annealing treatment (873 K for 24 h) and the other set to the modified, milder heat treatment (773 K for shorter time, e.g., 12–16 h) under identical atmospheres.
fields.structural_mediator: The relative proportion of homogeneous (matrix) fine L12 particles versus lamellar, cellular precipitates at grain boundaries.
fields.mechanism: By lowering the annealing temperature or reducing the annealing time, the diffusion rates are reduced such that long-range grain-boundary migration (a prerequisite for cellular precipitation) is suppressed. This promotes the homogeneous, coherent precipitation of nanoscale L12 particles in the FCC matrix. The resulting structure benefits high-temperature strength because of precipitate strengthening, maintains environmental resistance by preserving a continuous protective FCC matrix, ensures radiation tolerance via distributed defect sinks, and avoids the embrittlement associated with coarse lamellar features that could compromise cryogenic toughness.
fields.predicted_outcome: The modified heat treatment will yield an alloy with a higher density of fine, uniformly distributed L12 precipitates and fewer cellular, lamellar structures at grain boundaries compared to the baseline. This microstructure should exhibit improved high-temperature strength and resistance to irradiation-induced damage while retaining or enhancing cryogenic toughness relative to the baseline.
fields.baseline: An alloy annealed at 873 K for 24 h in which both homogeneous fine L12 particles and cellular (lamellar) precipitates at grain boundaries appear.
fields.boundary: The hypothesis is applicable in regimes where diffusion is sufficiently slowed to suppress grain-boundary migration but still permits homogeneous precipitation. It may not hold if the temperature is lowered too much or the time shortened excessively, which could result in incomplete precipitation and reduced overall strength.
fields.uncertainty: The precise trade-off between precipitation completeness and suppression of cellular precipitation, as well as the quantitative effect on radiation tolerance, remains to be determined.

falsification_experiment.design: Prepare two sets of samples from the same alloy composition using the baseline and modified annealing schedules. Characterize the precipitate morphology (TEM) and measure high-temperature mechanical properties, environmental corrosion resistance, radiation tolerance (via defect density measurements after irradiation), and cryogenic toughness.
measurements: TEM for precipitate size, distribution, and presence of grain-boundary lamellae
High-temperature creep or yield strength
Irradiation testing (e.g., ion irradiation followed by microstructural analysis)
Cryogenic impact tests
falsification_experiment.falsification_rule: If the modified heat treatment does not lead to a microstructure with significantly more uniformly distributed fine L12 precipitates and if the mechanical and resistance properties do not show improvement over the baseline, the hypothesis is falsified.

pool.label: C7
pool.builds_on: The mechanism builds on the PSSOS finding that precise atomic pair correlations govern formation energy and phase stability, suggesting that controlled thermal treatments targeting local order can directly modulate these correlations.
pool.what_is_new: This hypothesis goes beyond static high-throughput calculations by introducing a dynamic, cyclic annealing process as a processing parameter to fine-tune local atomic structure, rather than relying solely on compositional design.

fields.hypothesis: Cyclic low‐temperature annealing can optimize the local atomic pair correlations in Al–Co–Cr–Fe–Ni HEAs by gently driving local relaxation and strain relief without enabling long‐range diffusion, thereby stabilizing the disordered single‐phase structure and enhancing its multifunctional properties.
fields.material_initial_state: An as‐cast or conventionally annealed Al–Co–Cr–Fe–Ni HEA that exhibits slight local lattice distortions and incipient short‐range order as predicted by the PSSOS analysis.
fields.intervention: Subject the alloy to a series of low-temperature (e.g., 0.3–0.4 Tm) cyclic annealing treatments. Each cycle consists of a brief hold at a moderate temperature where only limited atomic mobility is allowed, followed by rapid cooling.
fields.conditions: Prepare two sets of samples with identical composition: one set receives a conventional isothermal annealing treatment, and the other undergoes cyclic annealing. The peak annealing temperature must be kept low enough to avoid long-range diffusion and secondary phase formation yet high enough to allow local atomic rearrangements.
fields.structural_mediator: Reduced local lattice distortions and a closer match of the atomic pair-correlation functions to that of an ideal disordered solid solution. The cyclic thermal excursions relieve local stress concentrations without triggering coarsening.
fields.mechanism: The repeated thermally driven, short-duration annealing cycles enable partial atomic rearrangement that relieves localized strain and minimizes deviations in pair correlations. This controlled local relaxation reduces the driving force for deleterious short-range ordering or clustering, leading to enhanced phase stability. A more uniform atomic environment promotes high-temperature strength, environmental resistance by reducing defect sites for corrosion, improved radiation tolerance through more homogeneous defect accommodation, and cryogenic toughness by eliminating brittle zones.
fields.predicted_outcome: Compared to a conventionally annealed sample, the cyclically annealed HEA should exhibit narrower XRD peak widths (indicating more uniform lattice parameters), lower calculated (or indirectly inferred) formation energies, and improved mechanical properties (e.g., enhanced cryogenic impact toughness and better high-temperature strength). The expected improvements in phase stability are predicted to be subtle (e.g., marginal shifts in formation energy on the order of tens of meV/atom), but measurable with high-precision techniques.
fields.baseline: The same composition of Al–Co–Cr–Fe–Ni HEA produced by a standard isothermal annealing schedule.
fields.boundary: The hypothesis applies for treatments at temperatures low enough to avoid triggering significant long-range diffusion or secondary phase precipitation. It is valid only within the nominal composition range (approximately 5–35 mol% per element) where the PSSOS method predictions hold.
fields.uncertainty: The quantitative magnitude of the improvement in pair-correlation matching and the corresponding property enhancements (e.g., toughness and high-temperature strength) is uncertain and may depend strongly on the exact annealing temperature, hold time, and cycle number.

falsification_experiment.design: Prepare two groups of Al–Co–Cr–Fe–Ni HEA samples with identical composition: one group receives conventional isothermal annealing, while the other is subjected to cyclic low-temperature annealing. Characterize both groups using high-resolution XRD, TEM (for local ordering), and mechanical testing (cryogenic impact and high-temperature tensile tests).
measurements: XRD to assess peak widths and lattice parameter uniformity
TEM for mapping local atomic arrangement and identifying short-range order
Differential scanning calorimetry (if applicable) to probe formation energies indirectly
Mechanical tests (tensile, impact) at cryogenic and high temperatures
falsification_experiment.falsification_rule: If cyclic annealing fails to produce statistically significant improvements in lattice uniformity, phase purity, or mechanical performance relative to the baseline, or if it unexpectedly promotes secondary phase formation or coarsening, the hypothesis is falsified.

pool.label: C8
pool.builds_on: the finding that the eutectic HEA’s excellent properties rely on its fine fcc/B2 lamellar microstructure (PMC4145285) and on established principles from superalloys where reactive element segregation improves interfacial stability.
pool.what_is_new: This hypothesis proposes using controlled Zr microalloying – supported by pre-test thermodynamic modeling – to enhance interfacial stability by modifying the low-energy interface itself, rather than only relying on bulk composition or process-induced structural features.

fields.hypothesis: Minor additions of zirconium (Zr) will preferentially segregate to the fcc/B2 eutectic interfaces in Al–Co–Cr–Fe–Ni HEAs, lowering the interfacial energy and curbing atomic diffusion. This interfacial decoration is expected to inhibit phase coarsening and compositional segregation under thermal, oxidative, and irradiation exposures, thereby retaining high-temperature strength, environmental resistance, radiation tolerance, and cryogenic toughness.
fields.material_initial_state: An as‐cast AlCoCrFeNi2.1 eutectic high-entropy alloy with a fine, regular lamellar fcc/B2 microstructure as produced by conventional casting.
fields.intervention: Introduce a minor addition (≈0.5 at.%) of Zr during the alloy melting stage to encourage its enrichment at the fcc/B2 interfaces.
fields.conditions: Prepare two sets of alloys – one baseline and one with Zr addition – and subject them to extended high-temperature aging (600–700°C), cyclic oxidation, simulated irradiation (e.g., ion irradiation), and cryogenic mechanical tests.
fields.structural_mediator: The formation of a Zr-rich interfacial layer that reduces interfacial energy and retards atomic diffusion along the fcc/B2 boundaries.
fields.mechanism: Thermodynamic calculations (via CALPHAD or ab initio methods) indicate that Zr exhibits a strong negative mixing enthalpy with elements in the NiAl-rich B2 phase and the fcc phase. This favorability drives Zr to segregate at the low-energy eutectic interfaces, where it further lowers the effective boundary energy, thus reducing atomic mobility and retarding coarsening processes. The stabilized interfaces maintain the composite lamellar microstructure under service conditions.
fields.predicted_outcome: The Zr-doped alloy will display a more chemically uniform and dimensionally stable lamellar structure over prolonged high-temperature and irradiation exposures, with measurable retention (or slight improvement) of high-temperature strength and cryogenic toughness compared to the Yb-free baseline.
fields.baseline: The as-cast AlCoCrFeNi2.1 eutectic HEA produced without Zr addition.
fields.boundary: Effective only for low-level Zr additions (below 1 at.%); higher concentrations risk forming separate Zr-rich intermetallic phases detrimental to mechanical performance.
fields.uncertainty: The precise extent of Zr segregation to the fcc/B2 interfaces and its quantifiable impact on diffusivity reduction and mechanical properties is not yet fully established.

falsification_experiment.design: Fabricate two sets of alloys—baseline AlCoCrFeNi2.1 and one with ≈0.5 at.% Zr addition—under identical casting conditions. Subject both to high-temperature aging (600–700°C) for extended durations, cyclic oxidation, and ion irradiation. Evaluate the microstructure (using TEM/atom probe tomography) for evidence of Zr segregation, measure diffusion profiles at the interfaces, and perform mechanical tests (tensile and cryogenic toughness).
measurements: Atom probe or high-resolution TEM/EDS mapping of fcc/B2 interfaces
Quantification of lamellar spacing and coarsening after aging
Mechanical property tests (tensile strength, fracture toughness, etc.)
Oxidation weight gain and defect density after irradiation
falsification_experiment.falsification_rule: If the Zr-doped alloy does not show significant Zr enrichment at the interfaces, if no measurable reduction in interfacial diffusivity or coarsening is observed, and if mechanical properties under thermal/irradiative and cryogenic conditions are statistically equivalent to or worse than the baseline, the hypothesis is falsified.

pool.label: C9
pool.builds_on: the original observation that a near-equilibrium eutectic microstructure is central to the alloy’s properties (PMC4145285) and leverages established principles of ordering kinetics from intermetallic systems.
pool.what_is_new: This hypothesis introduces a novel thermal treatment to actively enhance the atomic ordering at the fcc/B2 interfaces, offering an interfacial stabilization mechanism that is distinct from both compositional modifications and conventional thermomechanical treatments.

fields.hypothesis: A controlled isothermal annealing just below the eutectic reaction temperature will promote enhanced atomic ordering at the fcc/B2 phase interfaces. This ordering increases interface coherency, minimizes interfacial diffusion, and stabilizes the lamellar microstructure, thereby governing phase stability under combined high-temperature, irradiation, and cryogenic conditions.
fields.material_initial_state: The as‐cast AlCoCrFeNi2.1 eutectic HEA featuring a fine lamellar microstructure with coupled fcc and B2 phases.
fields.intervention: Apply a short-duration isothermal annealing treatment at a temperature slightly below the eutectic temperature (e.g., around 900°C) to promote atomic reordering at the phase boundaries without triggering significant coarsening.
fields.conditions: Compare annealed specimens with as-cast baselines under tests involving prolonged high-temperature exposure (600–700°C), cyclic oxidation, ion irradiation simulations, and mechanical testing at both elevated and cryogenic temperatures.
fields.structural_mediator: The development of a sharper, more coherent fcc/B2 interface with a higher degree of atomic ordering induced by the annealing treatment.
fields.mechanism: At an annealing temperature just below the eutectic liquidus, atomic mobility is sufficient to allow short-range reordering at the fcc/B2 interfaces without inducing significant coarsening. This reordering lowers the interfacial energy and enhances coherency, which in turn reduces the diffusion pathways that would normally lead to phase segregation and coarsening during service. A more ordered interface is expected to suppress elemental redistribution under thermal and irradiation stresses.
fields.predicted_outcome: Annealed alloys will exhibit sharper and more coherent interfaces, as evidenced by diffraction and atomic-scale imaging. Over extended aging and irradiation, these specimens should maintain finer lamellar spacing and exhibit less degradation in high-temperature strength and cryogenic toughness relative to the as-cast baseline.
fields.baseline: The unmodified, as-cast AlCoCrFeNi2.1 eutectic HEA.
fields.boundary: The treatment window is limited to temperatures that enhance ordering without crossing into regimes where phase transformations or significant coarsening occur. Duration must be carefully controlled to avoid deleterious microstructural changes.
fields.uncertainty: The quantitative improvement in interface ordering and its direct translation into mechanical property stabilization remain to be precisely determined.

falsification_experiment.design: Produce two sets of specimens, one as-cast and one subjected to the optimized isothermal annealing at ~900°C for a controlled short period. Following annealing, perform long-term high-temperature aging, cyclic oxidation, and irradiation tests. Use high-resolution TEM and XRD to assess interface ordering and coherency, and conduct mechanical tests (tensile, fracture, cryogenic ductility).
measurements: XRD profiles and TEM imaging to compare interface sharpness and ordering
Assessment of lamellar spacing and coarsening over aging tests
Mechanical properties (strength, toughness) under high-temperature and cryogenic conditions
Oxidation and irradiation damage evaluation
falsification_experiment.falsification_rule: If the annealed specimens do not show enhanced interfacial atomic ordering or improved coherency (as measured by TEM/XRD), and if no significant retardation of microstructural coarsening or improvement in mechanical performance is observed relative to the as-cast baseline, the hypothesis is falsified.

pool.label: C10
pool.builds_on: the paper’s demonstration that high surface free energy from ultrafine grains leads to improved oxidation behavior (PMC9026100::web::014) and literature on microstructural gradients in metals (TXT::wikipedia::Stainless_steel::011) that yield combined property benefits.
pool.what_is_new: This hypothesis proposes a deliberate engineering of a strain-gradient microstructure in Al–Co–Cr–Fe–Ni HEA via controlled high-pressure torsion to achieve a dual-layer architecture that simultaneously enhances surface oxidation protection and bulk phase stability—a strategy not explored in the original work.

fields.hypothesis: A gradient microstructure produced by controlled high‐pressure torsion (HPT) processing—yielding an ultrafine, high surface energy layer at the surface and a coarser, stable FCC bulk—governs phase stability by combining rapid protective oxide scale formation at the surface with robust bulk phase retention. This dual microstructure enhances high-temperature strength, radiation tolerance, and cryogenic toughness.
fields.material_initial_state: Al–Co–Cr–Fe–Ni HEA fabricated via conventional casting followed by severe plastic deformation, leading to a homogeneous ultrafine-grained microstructure with a high density of grain boundaries.
fields.intervention: Apply a controlled high-pressure torsion process with a designed strain gradient such that the surface experiences very high shear (resulting in nanocrystalline, high surface free energy structure) while the interior is subjected to lesser deformation (retaining a relatively coarser, stable FCC grain structure).
fields.conditions: Prepare two sets of samples: one processed to develop a gradient microstructure (with distinct surface and bulk zones) and one processed to a relatively homogeneous ultrafine microstructure. Subject both sets to high-temperature oxidation tests, ion irradiation (to simulate radiation effects), and mechanical evaluations at elevated and cryogenic temperatures.
fields.structural_mediator: A dual-phase microstructure consisting of a surface region with highly refined grains (providing enhanced surface free energy for rapid chemisorption of oxygen and protective oxide formation) and a bulk region with coarser, more stable FCC grains (providing superior mechanical integrity and radiation tolerance).
fields.mechanism: The gradient in deformation induced by HPT produces a tailored microstructural distribution. The ultrafine surface layer, with its high fraction of grain boundaries, promotes the rapid establishment of continuous, adherent protective oxide scales, while the relatively less deformed bulk retains a stable FCC phase that resists diffusion-driven phase transformations. This dual-architecture minimizes the propagation of deleterious phase changes under thermal stress and ion irradiation, thereby maintaining optimal mechanical properties across temperatures.
fields.predicted_outcome: Samples with the engineered gradient microstructure will show a thinner, more uniform and adherent oxide scale on the surface (measured via oxidation mass gain and SEM analysis), higher retention of the FCC phase in the bulk (as determined by XRD/EBSD), and superior mechanical performance (improved yield strength and toughness at high and cryogenic temperatures) as well as enhanced radiation tolerance compared to the homogeneous ultrafine-grained samples. The magnitude of improvement is expected to be significant relative to the baseline, although exact numerical gains are uncertain.
fields.baseline: A homogeneous ultrafine-grained HEA produced by uniform severe plastic deformation, which, while offering improved oxidation resistance, may suffer from bulk phase instability or lower toughness under irradiation or cryogenic conditions.
fields.boundary: The beneficial effects depend on precisely controlling the strain gradient; if the gradient is too steep, the bulk may inadvertently attain an ultrafine structure leading to possible inverse Hall-Petch softening, whereas too mild a gradient may not provide the desired surface protective properties.
fields.uncertainty: While the concept of strain-gradient-induced microstructural tailoring is supported by severe plastic deformation literature (e.g., PMC9026100 sections on microstructure), the optimal processing parameters and the exact interplay between surface and bulk phase stability in this HEA system remain to be precisely determined.

falsification_experiment.design: Prepare two groups of HEA samples: one with a deliberately induced gradient microstructure via tailored high-pressure torsion (with high strain at the surface and lower strain inside) and one with a homogeneous ultrafine-grained structure. Characterize the microstructure gradients using cross-sectional EBSD/TEM and determine oxidation kinetics, phase composition (FCC retention) via XRD, and mechanical properties (tensile, impact toughness at high and cryogenic temperatures) along with simulated radiation exposure.
measurements: Depth profile of grain size and grain boundary character using cross-sectional EBSD/TEM
Oxide scale thickness and uniformity via SEM/EDS after oxidation tests
Phase fraction (FCC vs. BCC/B2) using XRD analysis at different depths
Mechanical properties (yield strength, fracture toughness) at varied temperatures
Radiation-induced changes via post-irradiation microstructural assessment
falsification_experiment.falsification_rule: If the gradient microstructure samples do not exhibit a clearly distinct near-surface ultrafine grain layer with improved oxidation resistance and maintain a more stable FCC bulk as compared to the homogeneous samples—or if the mechanical and radiation performance does not significantly improve—then the hypothesis would be falsified.

pool.label: C11
pool.builds_on: the paper’s mechanism noting that cross-slip-induced strengthening dominates L12 precipitate behavior; here, the heat-treatment process is used to deliberately engineer the microstructure to maximize this mechanism in an HEA system.
pool.what_is_new: This hypothesis introduces a processing route adjustment (dual-step heat treatment) for Al–Co–Cr–Fe–Ni HEAs that is aimed at creating an optimized L12 nanoprecipitate network, rather than modifying composition, to govern phase stability and thus improve a combination of high-temperature strength, environmental resistance, radiation tolerance, and cryogenic toughness.

fields.hypothesis: A dual-step heat treatment, involving a high-temperature solution treatment followed by a controlled subsolvus aging, will promote a refined and coherent distribution of L12 nanoprecipitates in the Al–Co–Cr–Fe–Ni HEA. This tailored microstructure improves phase stability by enhancing cross-slip-induced dislocation locking and resisting coarsening under harsh thermal and environmental conditions.
fields.material_initial_state: An Al–Co–Cr–Fe–Ni high-entropy alloy produced by conventional melting with a predominantly single-phase disordered FCC microstructure.
fields.intervention: Replace the standard single-step homogenization with a dual-step process: first, a high-temperature solution treatment to dissolve any preexisting heterogeneities, and then a precisely controlled aging at a subsolvus temperature to induce nucleation and growth of fine, coherent L12 precipitates.
fields.conditions: Apply the dual-step heat treatment to a batch of HEA samples while maintaining another batch with conventional heat treatment as a control. Characterize phase evolution via DSC, XRD, and TEM. Subject both sets to mechanical testing across a temperature range (from cryogenic to high temperatures) and to simulated radiation and corrosive environments.
fields.structural_mediator: The dual-step heat treatment produces a fine, coherent dispersion of L12 nanoprecipitates that are intimately linked with the matrix via enhanced anti-phase boundaries. This distribution improves cross-slip-induced dislocation locking and retards precipitate coarsening, directly influencing overall phase stability.
fields.mechanism: Following insights from the paper where cross-slip-induced strengthening dominates the yield behavior, the dual-step process aims to tailor precipitate morphology such that dislocations are effectively pinned by a dense, coherent nanoprecipitate network. The subsolvus aging ensures that the precipitates remain at an optimum size and distribution, thereby maintaining phase stability and mechanical performance under variable service conditions including high temperature, radiation, and cryogenic stress.
fields.predicted_outcome: The dual-step heat-treated HEA should exhibit a higher density of uniformly sized L12 nanoprecipitates, leading to improved yield strength at high temperatures (with an expected enhancement similar to the 30–80% reported in related systems, subject to HEA complexities), better retention of phase integrity after prolonged thermal exposure, enhanced radiation resistance, and superior cryogenic toughness relative to the conventionally treated alloy.
fields.baseline: Al–Co–Cr–Fe–Ni HEA processed with a standard single-step homogenization and heat treatment.
fields.boundary: The benefits are expected provided that the aging temperature is carefully controlled to promote nucleation without excessive coarsening. If the dual-step scheme inadvertently coarsens the precipitates or leads to inhomogeneous distributions, the expected mechanism fails.
fields.uncertainty: The exact parameters (temperatures, durations) for optimal dual-step processing in an HEA system are not fully established, and the magnitude of enhancement may vary depending on the interplay of multiple alloying elements.

falsification_experiment.design: Prepare two groups of Al–Co–Cr–Fe–Ni HEA specimens: one processed by the conventional single-step heat treatment and one by the dual-step heat treatment (solution treatment plus controlled aging). Characterize the precipitate structure and distribution via TEM and XRD, and conduct mechanical testing (compression/tensile tests across a range of temperatures, irradiation exposure, and cryogenic toughness assessments).
measurements: TEM imaging for precipitate size and coherence
XRD for phase identification and ordering
Mechanical test data (yield strength, ductility) across temperature regimes
Environmental and radiation resistance tests
falsification_experiment.falsification_rule: If the dual-step heat-treated specimens do not demonstrate a finer, more coherent precipitate distribution coupled with improved stability and mechanical properties relative to the conventionally processed specimens, the hypothesis is falsified.

pool.label: C12
pool.builds_on: the paper’s demonstration that local transformation (fcc-to-BCC) is governed by ΔG_bcc–fcc and that local structural features (like interfaces) act as nucleation sites. This hypothesis leverages the concept of nanoprecipitation to modify local stress fields.
pool.what_is_new: This hypothesis introduces nanoprecipitate engineering via a minor Nb addition as a dual strategy to both strengthen the high-temperature FCC matrix and locally promote a controlled transformation under cryogenic conditions—a method not previously explored in the paper.

fields.hypothesis: A minor addition of niobium (Nb) can lead to the in situ formation of nanoscale, coherent Nb-rich precipitates that act as stress concentrators and dislocation pinning sites, thus locally reducing the energy barrier for FCC-to-BCC transformation during cryogenic deformation. This modification is expected to enhance transformation-induced plasticity while maintaining high-temperature strength and environmental resistance.
fields.material_initial_state: An Al–Co–Cr–Fe–Ni HEA that is conventionally processed to yield a homogeneous single-phase FCC structure with established high-temperature properties.
fields.intervention: Incorporate a controlled amount (e.g., 1–2 at.%) of Nb during casting such that subsequent homogenization and solution annealing foster the formation of finely dispersed, coherent Nb-rich nanoprecipitates.
fields.conditions: Produce two alloy series from the same baseline composition: one undoped and one with 1–2 at.% Nb. Use identical melting, homogenization, and solution annealing procedures conducive to forming nanoscale precipitates in the Nb-doped alloy. Characterize the precipitate size, volume fraction, and distribution via TEM. Finally, perform cryogenic tensile tests with in situ phase mapping (XRD/EBSD) and high-temperature mechanical evaluations.
fields.structural_mediator: The presence of coherent Nb-rich nanoprecipitates introduces local stress fields and dislocation pinning, which can lower the local ΔG_bcc–fcc barrier at the matrix–precipitate interfaces. These regions then become preferential sites for the nucleation of BCC martensite under cryogenic deformation, enhancing the transformation-induced plasticity effect. At high temperatures, the precipitates contribute to strengthening without disturbing the overall FCC matrix.
fields.mechanism: By adding Nb, the alloy partially decomposes into nanoscale precipitates that modify the local strain field and act as obstacles to dislocation motion. This localized stress concentration lowers the energy barrier for the FCC-to-BCC transformation at the matrix–precipitate interfaces, leading to controlled nucleation of BCC martensite during cryogenic deformation. Simultaneously, the precipitates offer conventional precipitation strengthening at high temperatures, aligning with the dual goals of maintaining high-temperature properties and enabling TRIP under cryogenic conditions.
fields.predicted_outcome: The Nb-doped alloy will display a more pronounced and spatially controlled formation of BCC martensite during cryogenic tensile testing, resulting in a steeper strain hardening curve and improved cryogenic toughness relative to the baseline. Additionally, high-temperature tests will confirm that the overall FCC matrix is maintained with enhanced strength due to precipitate hardening.
fields.baseline: The standard Al–Co–Cr–Fe–Ni HEA without Nb addition, which demonstrates limited stress-induced transformation under cryogenic loading.
fields.boundary: The beneficial impact is expected within a narrow Nb concentration window (around 1–2 at.%); higher levels may lead to excessive precipitation or formation of brittle intermetallic phases, while lower levels may not induce a measurable effect.
fields.uncertainty: The precise influence of nanoscale Nb-rich precipitates on the local ΔG_bcc–fcc remains to be quantitatively predicted via thermodynamic modeling and will need experimental verification to determine the optimal precipitate size and distribution.

falsification_experiment.design: Prepare two alloy series (one baseline and one with 1–2 at.% Nb) under identical processing conditions. Characterize the microstructure using TEM to confirm nanoprecipitate formation and distribution. Conduct cryogenic tensile tests with in situ phase mapping and compare the transformation behavior, and also perform high-temperature mechanical tests to ensure environmental and strength properties remain intact.
measurements: TEM analysis of Nb-rich precipitate size, volume fraction, and distribution
In situ XRD/EBSD phase evolution during cryogenic deformation
Mechanical testing (stress–strain curves) at cryogenic and high temperatures
falsification_experiment.falsification_rule: If the Nb-doped alloy does not exhibit a statistically significant increase in localized BCC nucleation and improved cryogenic plasticity compared to the baseline—or if high-temperature properties deteriorate due to unwanted phase formation—the hypothesis is falsified.

pool.label: C13
pool.builds_on: leverages the idea from the CrCoNi study that alloying elements and defect structures critically influence phase stability and deformation mechanisms, but introduces controlled minor alloying with boron to target grain-boundary energetics—a strategy not previously explored in this HEA system.
pool.what_is_new: This hypothesis proposes using trace boron additions to tailor the chemistry at internal interfaces, thereby suppressing deleterious phase nucleation and enhancing the beneficial deformation mechanisms, offering a new alloying strategy for stabilizing phase and multifunctional performance in Al–Co–Cr–Fe–Ni HEAs.

fields.hypothesis: The addition of a trace amount of boron (on the order of 0.3 atomic percent) in Al–Co–Cr–Fe–Ni HEAs will lead to preferential segregation of B at grain boundaries and dislocation cores, thereby reducing interfacial energies and impeding the nucleation of unwanted secondary phases, while at the same time enhancing deformation mechanisms (such as nano-twinning) that contribute to high-temperature strength and cryogenic toughness.
fields.material_initial_state: A conventionally processed, equiatomic Al–Co–Cr–Fe–Ni high-entropy alloy with unmodified grain-boundary chemistry and standard dislocation structures.
fields.intervention: Introduce a controlled minor addition of boron (e.g., approximately 0.3 at%) during melting, followed by identical homogenization, thermo-mechanical processing, and recrystallization as for the baseline alloy.
fields.conditions: All melting and processing steps are conducted in an inert atmosphere; the resulting alloys are then subjected to high-temperature aging, simulated irradiation, and mechanical testing at cryogenic temperatures.
fields.structural_mediator: Boron segregation at grain boundaries and dislocation cores is characterized using atom probe tomography (APT) or energy-filtered TEM, while changes in grain boundary character and local chemistry are further analyzed by EBSD and EDS. Phase stability is monitored by XRD.
fields.mechanism: The trace addition of boron preferentially segregates to high-energy sites such as grain boundaries and dislocation cores during processing, lowering the boundary energy and stabilizing the FCC matrix. This reduced interfacial energy diminishes the thermodynamic driving force for the nucleation of brittle intermetallic or oxide phases. Moreover, boron may help anchor dislocations, promoting the formation and stability of deformation-induced nano-twins that enhance toughness at low temperatures.
fields.predicted_outcome: B-doped HEA samples will display a reduction in the formation of undesired secondary phases after high-temperature or irradiation exposure, and mechanical testing will reveal enhanced high-temperature strength and improved fracture toughness and ductility at cryogenic temperatures relative to boron-free counterparts.
fields.baseline: A standard equiatomic Al–Co–Cr–Fe–Ni HEA without boron addition, processed under identical conditions.
fields.boundary: This effect is expected for very low boron additions (typically <0.5 at%) where boron segregates without forming separate boride phases. Excessive boron could lead to precipitate formation that may adversely affect ductility.
fields.uncertainty: The precise influence of 0.3 at% B on grain-boundary energetics and its balance with potential precipitation effects require further quantitative determination.

falsification_experiment.design: Produce two sets of samples: one with ~0.3 at% boron addition and one without. Characterize boron segregation at grain boundaries and dislocation cores using APT or TEM-EDS. Expose both sets to accelerated high-temperature aging and simulated irradiation, then assess phase stability (via XRD and TEM). Finally, conduct tensile and fracture toughness tests at high-temperature and cryogenic conditions.
measurements: Elemental segregation at boundaries (APT, TEM-EDS)
Phase stability (XRD, TEM)
Mechanical properties (tensile strength, fracture toughness)
falsification_experiment.falsification_rule: If the boron-doped samples do not exhibit a significant reduction in the formation of intermetallic or oxide phases, or if there is no measurable improvement in mechanical properties compared to the boron-free baseline, the hypothesis is falsified.

top3.builds_on: The paper’s observation of both homogeneous and cellular precipitation in the HEA and the background understanding that heat treatment parameters critically affect precipitation mechanisms.
top3.what_is_new: It proposes a specific heat treatment modification to decouple the beneficial fine-particle precipitation from the deleterious cellular (grain-boundary) precipitation, with direct implications for balancing high-temperature and cryogenic performance.

fields.hypothesis: Tailoring the annealing heat treatment to favor homogeneous nucleation of fine L12 precipitates over grain-boundary cellular precipitation will stabilize the FCC matrix and yield a microstructure that balances high-temperature strength with improved cryogenic toughness and environmental resistance.
fields.material_initial_state: An Al–Co–Cr–Fe–Ni HEA that is initially single-phase FCC after rapid quenching, similar to the state reported in the referenced paper.
fields.intervention: Modify the annealing schedule by reducing the isothermal holding temperature (e.g., from 873 K to a lower temperature such as 773 K) or reducing holding time to suppress the kinetics of grain-boundary migration and cellular precipitation, thereby promoting homogeneous fine L12 precipitation.
fields.conditions: Prepare parallel samples from the same alloy batch; subject one set to the baseline annealing treatment (873 K for 24 h) and the other set to the modified, milder heat treatment (773 K for shorter time, e.g., 12–16 h) under identical atmospheres.
fields.structural_mediator: The relative proportion of homogeneous (matrix) fine L12 particles versus lamellar, cellular precipitates at grain boundaries.
fields.mechanism: By lowering the annealing temperature or reducing the annealing time, the diffusion rates are reduced such that long-range grain-boundary migration (a prerequisite for cellular precipitation) is suppressed. This promotes the homogeneous, coherent precipitation of nanoscale L12 particles in the FCC matrix. The resulting structure benefits high-temperature strength because of precipitate strengthening, maintains environmental resistance by preserving a continuous protective FCC matrix, ensures radiation tolerance via distributed defect sinks, and avoids the embrittlement associated with coarse lamellar features that could compromise cryogenic toughness.
fields.predicted_outcome: The modified heat treatment will yield an alloy with a higher density of fine, uniformly distributed L12 precipitates and fewer cellular, lamellar structures at grain boundaries compared to the baseline. This microstructure should exhibit improved high-temperature strength and resistance to irradiation-induced damage while retaining or enhancing cryogenic toughness relative to the baseline.
fields.baseline: An alloy annealed at 873 K for 24 h in which both homogeneous fine L12 particles and cellular (lamellar) precipitates at grain boundaries appear.
fields.boundary: The hypothesis is applicable in regimes where diffusion is sufficiently slowed to suppress grain-boundary migration but still permits homogeneous precipitation. It may not hold if the temperature is lowered too much or the time shortened excessively, which could result in incomplete precipitation and reduced overall strength.
fields.uncertainty: The precise trade-off between precipitation completeness and suppression of cellular precipitation, as well as the quantitative effect on radiation tolerance, remains to be determined.

fields.hypothesis: Phase stability is governed by a temperature‐dependent competition between short-range ordering driven by dominant pair interactions (e.g., Al–Ni clustering) and the mixing entropy that stabilizes a random solid solution. In practice, holding the alloy isothermally at temperatures below the spinodal temperature (~840 K) promotes clustering, whereas maintaining high processing temperatures or rapid quenching preserves disorder. This balance ultimately affects high-temperature strength and oxidation (environmental) resistance.
fields.material_initial_state: A melt‐quenched Al–Co–Cr–Fe–Ni HEA (e.g., with Al mole fraction x = 0.1) in its metastable single‐phase FCC (A1) state that exhibits evidence of Al–Ni driven clustering as indicated by SRO parameters.
fields.intervention: Prepare two sets of identical HEA samples. For one group, apply an isothermal hold (annealing) at a temperature below ~840 K (e.g., 750 K) for a controlled duration to promote atomic clustering. For the other group, either rapidly quench from the melt or anneal at a temperature moderately above 840 K to maintain a more random disordered state.
fields.conditions: Identical composition (Al0.1CrCoFeNi) and processing history except for the controlled thermal treatment; testing to be performed at room and elevated temperatures (e.g., 300–700 K) for mechanical (flow stress) and oxidation resistance assessments.
fields.structural_mediator: The degree of short-range order (SRO) as quantified by pair correlation functions (e.g., intensity of Al–Ni and Al–Al peaks) measured via diffraction or atom probe techniques.
fields.mechanism: At temperatures below the spinodal threshold, the favorable chemical interchange energies (as evidenced in the KKR-CPA analysis, PMC4976365::web::007) overcome the mixing entropy, driving clustering of like pairs. In contrast, rapid quenching or annealing above this threshold preserves a more homogeneous atomic distribution. The local atomic arrangement influences free volume distribution and potential nucleation sites for oxidation, thereby impacting high-temperature mechanical strength and environmental resistance.
fields.predicted_outcome: Samples annealed below 840 K will show enhanced clustering (stronger Al–Ni and Al–Al pair peaks) and may exhibit slightly reduced high-temperature flow stress and lower oxidation resistance compared to the rapidly quenched or high-temperature held samples. The baseline (rapidly quenched) samples are predicted to have a more uniform disordered structure with improved performance in high-temperature environments.
fields.baseline: Al0.1CrCoFeNi HEA processed by rapid quenching, retaining the high-temperature disordered (entropy-stabilized) state.
fields.boundary: This temperature-dependent mechanism applies to the single-phase FCC (A1) regime with low Al content (x = 0.1) and assumes that thermal treatments do not trigger full phase separation or induce unwanted secondary phases beyond a limited clustering regime.
fields.uncertainty: The quantitative differences in mechanical or oxidation properties between the two states may be modest, and the precise temperature window over which the crossover occurs requires refinement; current support is robust for clustering trends but less so for direct property correlations.

top3.builds_on: The mechanism builds on the PSSOS finding that precise atomic pair correlations govern formation energy and phase stability, suggesting that controlled thermal treatments targeting local order can directly modulate these correlations.
top3.what_is_new: This hypothesis goes beyond static high-throughput calculations by introducing a dynamic, cyclic annealing process as a processing parameter to fine-tune local atomic structure, rather than relying solely on compositional design.

fields.hypothesis: Cyclic low‐temperature annealing can optimize the local atomic pair correlations in Al–Co–Cr–Fe–Ni HEAs by gently driving local relaxation and strain relief without enabling long‐range diffusion, thereby stabilizing the disordered single‐phase structure and enhancing its multifunctional properties.
fields.material_initial_state: An as‐cast or conventionally annealed Al–Co–Cr–Fe–Ni HEA that exhibits slight local lattice distortions and incipient short‐range order as predicted by the PSSOS analysis.
fields.intervention: Subject the alloy to a series of low-temperature (e.g., 0.3–0.4 Tm) cyclic annealing treatments. Each cycle consists of a brief hold at a moderate temperature where only limited atomic mobility is allowed, followed by rapid cooling.
fields.conditions: Prepare two sets of samples with identical composition: one set receives a conventional isothermal annealing treatment, and the other undergoes cyclic annealing. The peak annealing temperature must be kept low enough to avoid long-range diffusion and secondary phase formation yet high enough to allow local atomic rearrangements.
fields.structural_mediator: Reduced local lattice distortions and a closer match of the atomic pair-correlation functions to that of an ideal disordered solid solution. The cyclic thermal excursions relieve local stress concentrations without triggering coarsening.
fields.mechanism: The repeated thermally driven, short-duration annealing cycles enable partial atomic rearrangement that relieves localized strain and minimizes deviations in pair correlations. This controlled local relaxation reduces the driving force for deleterious short-range ordering or clustering, leading to enhanced phase stability. A more uniform atomic environment promotes high-temperature strength, environmental resistance by reducing defect sites for corrosion, improved radiation tolerance through more homogeneous defect accommodation, and cryogenic toughness by eliminating brittle zones.
fields.predicted_outcome: Compared to a conventionally annealed sample, the cyclically annealed HEA should exhibit narrower XRD peak widths (indicating more uniform lattice parameters), lower calculated (or indirectly inferred) formation energies, and improved mechanical properties (e.g., enhanced cryogenic impact toughness and better high-temperature strength). The expected improvements in phase stability are predicted to be subtle (e.g., marginal shifts in formation energy on the order of tens of meV/atom), but measurable with high-precision techniques.
fields.baseline: The same composition of Al–Co–Cr–Fe–Ni HEA produced by a standard isothermal annealing schedule.
fields.boundary: The hypothesis applies for treatments at temperatures low enough to avoid triggering significant long-range diffusion or secondary phase precipitation. It is valid only within the nominal composition range (approximately 5–35 mol% per element) where the PSSOS method predictions hold.
fields.uncertainty: The quantitative magnitude of the improvement in pair-correlation matching and the corresponding property enhancements (e.g., toughness and high-temperature strength) is uncertain and may depend strongly on the exact annealing temperature, hold time, and cycle number.

falsification_experiment.design: Prepare two groups of Al–Co–Cr–Fe–Ni HEA samples with identical composition: one group receives conventional isothermal annealing, while the other is subjected to cyclic low-temperature annealing. Characterize both groups using high-resolution XRD, TEM (for local ordering), and mechanical testing (cryogenic impact and high-temperature tensile tests).
measurements: XRD to assess peak widths and lattice parameter uniformity
TEM for mapping local atomic arrangement and identifying short-range order
Differential scanning calorimetry (if applicable) to probe formation energies indirectly

falsification_experiment.falsification_rule: If cyclic annealing fails to produce statistically significant improvements in lattice uniformity, phase purity, or mechanical performance relative to the baseline, or if it unexpectedly promotes secondary phase formation or coarsening, the hypothesis is falsified.
